prompt: What happens to a message in a queue once its consumer acknowledges it?

choices.text: The broker deletes it, since the work is done
choices.why: Right. The queue's model is work, and finished work is not kept.

choices.text: It stays for the seven-day retention
choices.why: That is the log's behaviour.

choices.text: It moves to the next consumer in the group, so it is read twice
choices.why: In a queue each message goes to one consumer.

choices.text: It is copied to every other queue bound to the exchange
choices.why: Copies are made when the message is published, not acknowledged.

prompt: An analytics team wants to read last month's `OrderPlaced` events, which three services have already processed. Which broker model makes that possible?
hint: Which one keeps messages after they are read?

choices.text: A queue, if the analytics team declares its own queue now
choices.why: A queue declared now receives only what is published from now on.

choices.text: A log, with retention covering a month
choices.why: Right. A new reader can start from the oldest retained message.

choices.text: Either, since both keep messages until every consumer has read them
choices.why: A queue deletes on acknowledgement.

choices.text: Neither; past events are gone in both
choices.why: A log keeps them for its retention period.

prompt: Match each statement to the model it describes.
hint: The table at the end of the section.

pairs.left: the broker tracks each message's state
the broker tracks each reader's offset

prompt: In the lab, how many mebibytes did the Kafka container use at rest, rounded to the nearest whole number?
Why does `docker compose up -d` start the two brokers and not the `tools` service?
hint: Look at the line under `tools` in `compose.yaml`.

choices.text: The tools image failed to build
choices.why: It builds; it is simply not started by `up`.

choices.text: Compose starts at most two services at a time
choices.why: There is no such limit.

choices.text: It is in a profile, which `up` skips
choices.why: Right. `docker compose run tools …` builds and runs it when a script is needed.

choices.text: It depends on Kafka, which is not ready yet
choices.why: It depends on RabbitMQ, and that is not why it is left out.

prompt: In RabbitMQ, where does a publisher send a message?

choices.text: Straight to the queue of the service that needs it
choices.why: A publisher never sends to a queue.

choices.text: To the consumer, which forwards it to its queue
choices.why: Consumers read from queues; they do not forward.

choices.text: To an exchange, with a routing key
choices.why: Right. Bindings decide which queues get a copy.

choices.text: To a partition chosen by the hash of its key
choices.why: That is Kafka's model.

prompt: Match each exchange type to what it delivers to.

pairs.right: queues bound with exactly the routing key
queues whose pattern matches, with * and #
every bound queue, whatever the key

right_distractors: the queue with the fewest messages

prompt: A queue is bound to a topic exchange with `order.*`. Which routing key does NOT reach it?

choices.text: `order.placed`
choices.why: One word after `order.`, so it matches.

choices.text: `order.refunded`
choices.why: One word after `order.`, so it matches.

choices.text: `order.item.added`
choices.why: Right. That is two words after `order.`; `order.#` would match it.

choices.text: `order.cancelled`
choices.why: One word after `order.`, so it matches.

prompt: Quitanda adds a loyalty service that must receive every order. What changes in RabbitMQ, and what changes in the publisher?

choices.text: A new exchange for loyalty, and the publisher sends to both
choices.why: One exchange serves every interested queue.

choices.text: A new queue and binding; nothing in the publisher
choices.why: Right. The publisher knows only the exchange.

choices.text: Nothing in RabbitMQ; the publisher adds a third routing key
choices.why: Without a queue bound, the messages would go nowhere.

choices.text: The e-mail queue is shared with loyalty, so they compete for messages
choices.why: Competing consumers would each get some orders, not all.

prompt: Two orders were published before any queue existed. What became of them?

choices.text: They waited in the exchange until the queues were declared
choices.why: An exchange holds no messages.

choices.text: They were dropped, and the publisher was never told
choices.why: Right. No binding matched, so they went nowhere.

choices.text: They were rejected, and `publish.py` raised an error
choices.why: `publish.py` printed them as published.

choices.text: They were delivered to the first consumer that connected
choices.why: Messages that were dropped reach nobody.

prompt: After `publish.py 6 7`, how many messages did the warehouse queue hold?
hint: Four nobody had read, plus six.

prompt: Two consumers shared the warehouse queue. What did the output show about order?

choices.text: The orders were handled strictly in the order they were published
choices.why: Order 10 was printed before order 9.

choices.text: Order 10 was handled and printed before order 9
choices.why: Right. Competing consumers do not keep the order of the queue.

choices.text: Each consumer handled every order, once each
choices.why: Each order was handled by one consumer.

choices.text: One consumer handled them all and the other none
choices.why: The two hostnames alternate in the output.

prompt: What does `prefetch_count=1` change for the two warehouse consumers?
hint: How many unacknowledged messages may each hold?

choices.text: Each message is delivered to both consumers
choices.why: That would be two queues, not two consumers.

choices.text: Messages are delivered in strict order
choices.why: It does not make two workers keep order.

choices.text: One message at a time each, the next after the ack
choices.why: Right, so the work spreads instead of piling on whoever connected first.

choices.text: Only one consumer may be connected at a time
choices.why: Both were connected and both worked.

prompt: What decides which partition a Kafka message is written to?

choices.text: The consumer group that will read it
choices.why: Producers do not know which groups will read.

choices.text: Its key
choices.why: Right: the same key, the same partition.

choices.text: The partition with the fewest messages at that moment
choices.why: Placement follows the key, not the load.

choices.text: A binding pattern on the topic
choices.why: Kafka has no bindings.

prompt: A consumer group has four consumers reading a topic with three partitions. What does the fourth consumer do?
hint: A partition is read by one consumer of a group.

choices.text: It waits idle until another one leaves
choices.why: Right. Parallelism is capped by the number of partitions.

choices.text: Reads a copy of every partition, as a backup
choices.why: A group divides partitions; it does not copy them.

choices.text: Shares partition 0 with another consumer
choices.why: A partition is read by one consumer of a group at a time.

choices.text: Creates a fourth partition for itself
choices.why: Consumers cannot create partitions.

prompt: Exactly which ordering does Kafka promise?

choices.text: The order of the whole topic, for every consumer
choices.why: Across partitions there is no order.

choices.text: The order of each consumer group's reads
choices.why: The promise is about partitions, not groups.

choices.text: The order of the producer's clock timestamps
choices.why: Timestamps play no part in placement.

choices.text: Within a partition, and none across partitions
choices.why: Right. Choosing the key decides what is kept in order.

prompt: The position of a message within its partition, starting at 0, is called its ___.
hint: Each consumer group stores one per partition.

prompt: In the lab, why did the consumer print ana's orders before bruno's order 2, although order 2 was produced before order 3?

choices.text: Kafka sorts messages by key before delivering them
choices.why: There is no sorting; the partitions are read one after the other.

choices.text: The producer sent order 3 first by mistake
choices.why: The producer sent them in the order of the input.

choices.text: They are in different partitions, and nothing orders across them
choices.why: Right. Within each partition the order held.

choices.text: Order 2 was lost and written again later
choices.why: Nothing was lost; offsets 0 to 2 of partition 2 are all there.

prompt: After the two extra orders, what was the email group's total lag across the three partitions?
A group's lag on one topic grows by a few hundred messages every hour. What does that say?

choices.text: The topic is losing messages
choices.why: The messages are there; the group is behind them.

choices.text: The producer is sending duplicates
choices.why: Lag counts unread messages, not duplicates.

choices.text: The retention period is too long
choices.why: Retention does not change how fast a group reads.

choices.text: The consumers are not keeping up
choices.why: Right, and the oldest unread message gets older by the minute.

prompt: Match each column of `kafka-consumer-groups --describe` to what it means.

pairs.right: where the group will read next
where the next message will be written
how many messages the group has not read

right_distractors: how many consumers are in the group

prompt: The new group `warehouse` read the topic from the beginning. How many messages did it read?
What did the `warehouse` group's reading do to the `email` group?

choices.text: It moved the email group's offsets to the end
choices.why: Each group stores its own offsets.

choices.text: It removed the messages the email group had not read yet
choices.why: Reading removes nothing from a log.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. Each group has its own position in the same log.

choices.text: It doubled the email group's lag
choices.why: Lag depends only on the email group's position and the log's end.

prompt: The e-mail service fixed a bug and its group's offsets were reset to the earliest. What must be true of the e-mail consumer before that is safe?
hint: It will act on old messages as if they were new.

choices.text: Its consumers must be running while the offsets are reset
choices.why: The tool refuses to reset a group with active consumers.

choices.text: The topic must have only one partition
choices.why: Resetting works on any number of partitions.

choices.text: Running twice on one message must be safe
choices.why: Right, idempotency, which is lesson 7.

choices.text: The producer must send the messages again
choices.why: The messages are still in the log; nothing is sent again.

prompt: A consumer of an SQS queue takes 45 seconds to handle a message, and the visibility timeout is 30 seconds. What happens?
hint: What does the message do when the timeout passes before it is deleted?

choices.text: SQS waits for the consumer to finish, however long it takes
choices.why: The timeout does not wait for anyone.

choices.text: The message is deleted after 30 seconds as failed
choices.why: It becomes visible again rather than deleted.

choices.text: The consumer is disconnected from the queue for good
choices.why: Nothing disconnects it; the message simply reappears.

choices.text: It reappears, and another consumer handles it too
choices.why: Right. The timeout must be longer than the slowest normal handling.

prompt: The queue where messages go after failing a set number of times, for a person to look at, is called a ___ queue.
Which of these keeps order within a group of messages, the way a key does in Kafka?
hint: A FIFO queue and its message groups.

choices.text: An SQS standard queue
choices.why: Standard queues make no promise of order.

choices.text: An SQS FIFO queue
choices.why: Right, per message group.

choices.text: A RabbitMQ fanout exchange
choices.why: An exchange routes; it does not order.

choices.text: Any dead-letter queue
choices.why: A dead-letter queue holds failures; order is not its job.

prompt: According to the lesson, what is the first question in choosing a broker?

choices.text: Are the messages work to be done or a record of what happened?
choices.why: Right. The answer picks a family.

choices.text: Which broker has the most stars on GitHub?
choices.why: Popularity says nothing about fit.

choices.text: Which language are the services written in?
choices.why: Both brokers have clients for every common language.

choices.text: How many messages per second will there be on the first day?
choices.why: Volume matters later; the model comes first.

prompt: Why does Quitanda put its order events in a log and its pick list in a queue?
hint: Who wants the orders later, and who wants a pick list replayed?

choices.text: Logs are faster for small messages and queues for large ones
choices.why: Size is not the reason given.

choices.text: The warehouse team only knows RabbitMQ
choices.why: The reason is in the messages, not the team.

choices.text: A system may only run one broker of each kind
choices.why: Running both is normal; that is not the reason.

choices.text: Orders will be read again by readers not yet written; picks are work, retried per item
choices.why: Right.

prompt: Put the pieces a RabbitMQ message passes through in order, from the publisher to the consumer.
items: The publisher sends it with a routing key
The exchange compares the key with its bindings
Each matching queue stores a copy
A consumer takes it and acknowledges it

prompt: The fraud team, created this month, needs every `OrderPlaced` from the past week to train a model. Orders go through RabbitMQ today. What does the lesson suggest?
hint: Which model keeps messages for readers that come later?

choices.text: Bind a new queue for fraud; it will receive last week's orders
choices.why: A queue receives only what is published after it is bound.

choices.text: Publish orders to a log as well, with retention long enough
choices.why: Right. A new group can then start from the past.

choices.text: Ask the e-mail service to forward its queue to fraud
choices.why: The e-mail queue's messages were deleted when acknowledged.

choices.text: Reset the RabbitMQ queue's offsets to last week
choices.why: Queues have no offsets to reset.
